subject: surgery
title: Tumour Markers and Surgery for Testicular Cancer

steps.tx: A hormone subunit produced by some germ cell tumours used as a marker is **beta-hCG**. Human chorionic gonadotropin rises in choriocarcinoma and some seminomas. Falling levels after treatment confirm response, while rising levels warn of recurrence. Pure seminoma never raises alpha fetoprotein, so a raised alpha fetoprotein reclassifies the tumour even if biopsy reads seminoma.
steps.say: Beta-hCG marks some germ cell tumours, and falling levels confirm treatment response.

steps.tx: Removal of the testis through a groin incision with high cord division is **high inguinal orchidectomy**. Approaching through the groin avoids disturbing lymph drainage patterns of the scrotum. The specimen gives the exact tumour type for staging. Cutting the cord high, at the internal ring, before handling the testis prevents squeezing tumour cells into veins.
steps.say: High inguinal orchidectomy removes the testis through the groin and gives the exact tumour type.

steps.tx: Surgical clearance of nodes beside the great abdominal vessels is **retroperitoneal lymph node dissection**. It treats residual or relapsing nodal disease after chemotherapy in selected patients. Nerve sparing technique protects ejaculation where possible. Residual masses over 3 centimetres after chemotherapy are the usual target, and surgery within six weeks of chemotherapy is preferred.
steps.say: Retroperitoneal node dissection clears nodes beside the great vessels for residual disease after chemotherapy.

steps.tx: Marker levels measured before and after orchidectomy guide **risk stratification**. Persistently raised markers imply remaining disease even with normal scans. Such patients usually receive chemotherapy rather than surveillance alone. Marker half life matters: beta-hCG should halve every one to two days after the testis comes out, and slower falls mean residual disease.
steps.say: Persistently raised markers after orchidectomy imply remaining disease and usually lead to chemotherapy.

steps.tx: A rapidly growing haemorrhagic tumour type with very high beta-hCG is **choriocarcinoma**. It spreads early through the bloodstream to lungs and brain. Chemotherapy is urgent and usually highly effective. Beta-hCG can exceed one million international units per litre, and bleeding into lung or brain deposits is the feared early event.
steps.say: Choriocarcinoma grows fast, bleeds, spreads through blood, and needs urgent chemotherapy.

steps.tx: Long term follow up after testicular cancer treatment is called **surveillance protocol**. It combines marker checks, examination and interval imaging over years. Most relapses occur within two years and remain curable when caught early. Chest imaging is added because the lungs are the first filter for blood borne spread from the testis.
steps.say: Surveillance combines markers, examination and imaging, and most early relapses remain curable.

steps.tx: Fertility preservation should be discussed before chemotherapy, centred on **sperm banking**. Chemotherapy can reduce sperm production for years. Offering storage before treatment protects future family choices. A single cycle of carboplatin chemotherapy can halve sperm counts for a year, so banking is offered even for early stage disease.
steps.say: Sperm banking before chemotherapy protects future fertility choices for young men.

steps.tx: Scrotal violation by biopsy through the skin changes drainage and worsens control, hence the rule of **never biopsying through scrotum**. Suspected tumours are removed whole through the groin instead. This principle is absolute in testicular cancer surgery. A scrotal scar from a breach is treated by removing that side of the scrotum at definitive surgery to regain control.
steps.say: Never biopsy a testicular tumour through the scrotum; remove it whole through the groin instead.

steps.tx: Overall cure rates exceed ninety five percent in early disease, reflecting excellent **treatment outcomes**. Even widespread disease is often curable with chemotherapy. This success makes early presentation and full treatment completion vital. Stage one seminoma under surveillance relapses in about 15 to 20 percent, almost always in retroperitoneal nodes within three years.
steps.say: Early testicular cancer cures exceed ninety five percent, making early presentation vital.
